newsitem.title: INDIA: Mother Teresa a byword for devotion to destitute.
newsitem.headline: Mother Teresa a byword for devotion to destitute.

text.p: Mother Teresa, who is to be succeeded by a Hindu convert on Thursday to head the Roman Catholic order she founded nearly 50 years ago, has won hearts the world over for her devotion to the poor and dying.

The 86-year-old nun of Albanian descent was watching quietly in the Indian city of Calcutta as Sister Nirmala was elected by an assembly of nuns as the superior-general of the Missionaries of Charity, the order Mother Teresa founded in 1948.
Sister Nirmala, 23 years younger than the order's ailing founder, was expected to inject vigour into the organisation's leadership but not eclipse the charismatic Mother Teresa.
The 1979 Nobel Peace Prize winner, who fought lung and heart ailments before deciding to retire, has done most of her work in the teeming slums of Calcutta.
Known as the "Saint of the Gutters", she became an international byword for devotion to the poor, destitute and dying as the lonely task she began in the city grew bigger.
Mother Teresa, whose order has about 4,500 nuns operating in more than 80 countries, has said apart from poverty and hunger, the world's major problems are loneliness and neglect.
The order now feeds about 500,000 families each year, teaches 20,000 children and treats 90,000 lepers.
But, like most world icons, Mother Teresa has been no stranger to criticism and has drawn some unflattering comments for her conservative beliefs and an tolerance to suffering.
Mother Teresa won the Nobel prize for bringing hope and dignity to millions of unwanted people. "The poor must know that we love them," was her simple message after receiving the award.
She has received dozens of international laurels. Last year, President Bill Clinton approved honorary U.S. citizenship for her, an honour shared by only four other foreigners.
Bowed and gnarled, her head shrouded by a sari, she has became a familiar symbol of selfless work.
Mother Teresa's health deteriorated in the 1980s. In 1989, she was fitted with a pacemaker.
A year later, the Vatican announced she was resigning as head of her order. Delegates from the order arrived in Calcutta to elect a successor, but persuaded her to stay on.
But her health kept failing. Between 1991 and 1995, she was treated for heart and lung problems, pneumonia and two separate bone fractures.

Last year, she spent three weeks in hospital for heart trouble, malaria and pneumonia in August and September, and later fell off a chair and hit her head. She was in hospital again in November for surgery to unblock coronary arteries.
Her order then agreed she must retire.

Mother Teresa was born Agnes Goinxha Bejaxhiu to Albanian parents in Skopje, in what was then Serbia, on August 27, 1910. She became a Loretto nun at 18. She came later to Calcutta from Dublin and started work as a convent school teacher.
She took the name Teresa, after France's Saint Therese of the Child Jesus. In mainly Hindu India, she was simply "Mother".

In 1994, a controversial television documentary on Britain's Channel 4 called "Hell's Angel" questioned the worth of Mother Teresa's charity work in India's slums and called the media myth around her a mixture of "hyperbole and credulity".
Catholics and others around the world rose to defend her.
